label: Inside the switch module
value: A 800G twin-port optical module, opened up: its footprint drawn to its published size, its layers pulled apart vertically, its parts representative. This scenario’s switch module: OSFP 800G 2xDR4 (NVIDIA MMS4X00), the module in the leaf and spine switches’ cages. It carries two 400G links: one shared eight-lane DSP serves a representative photonics chip, with eight 100G transmit channels grouped on one side and eight receive channels on the other. Four channels in each direction feed each optical port. The internal placement and separate analog chips are representative, not a documented teardown. The DGX H100 servers take the flat-top version of this module; the switches take this finned one. The Switch side · NIC side toggle changes the end named, not the drawing. Everything that turns the host’s electrical lanes into light, and back, is inside. The other toggle also shows a half-retimed (LRO) version, with the DSP on transmit only, and the LPO version, with no DSP.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: Inside the switch module
value: This scenario’s switch module, OSFP 800G 2xDR4: one eight-channel transmit bank and one eight-channel receive bank at 100G per lane, serving two 400G optical ports. Internal placement and chip partitioning are representative. Out: the host’s lanes, the shared eight-lane DSP, a driver, electrical connections to the modulators, which put each lane onto the lasers’ light, then glass fiber to the connector. In: fiber from the connector to a photodiode, electrical connections to the TIA, the DSP, and back to the host.
reason: Recertified 10/08/2026: supported with a disclosed assumption or limit. The signal path is the textbook transmit and receive chain; placement is stated as representative.

label: Inside the switch module
value: The DSP is the major heat source. Its heat crosses a gap pad into the shell and leaves through the fins, in the air the switch or server blows past its cages. The driver, TIA and lasers make less; heat is drawn on a log scale, so each 10× in power is 5× the motion.
reason: Recertified 10/08/2026: supported with a disclosed assumption or limit. The log-scale heat drawing is the labeled assumption heat-visual-scale: exponent log10(5) = 0.699, so 10x power is 5.0x motion. DSP as the major source follows the allocations listed in that assumption.

label: Coherent optics
value: Follow the separately packaged electronics and optical assemblies: DSP → driver IC → IQ modulator on transmit; receiver photodiodes → TIA IC → DSP on receive. The driver and TIA carry electrical signals, not light. One laser feeds the modulator and the receiver’s local oscillator. This discrete package arrangement is a design assumption, not a teardown of a specific product.

label: interhall
value: About 204k strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other.

label: line

label: mpt

label: interhall
value: About 2.0 million strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: optics

label: line
value: Lattice towers carry two three-phase circuits of bundled aluminum conductor, with a shield wire on top to take lightning. At 345 kV the whole 5 GW campus rides on ≈4,400 A per phase on each circuit, which is why power travels far at high voltage. A campus this big would take several circuits, or 500 kV.

label: mpt
value: Oil-filled transformers, each the weight of a loaded freight car, step the line down to the campus distribution voltage. Radiators and fans shed their heat; concrete fire walls keep one fire from taking the others. Three are drawn; this campus needs 19.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: interhall
value: About 10.2 million strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: ductbank

label: optics

label: Inside the switch module
value: A 800G twin-port optical module, opened up: its footprint drawn to its published size, its layers pulled apart vertically, its parts representative. This scenario’s switch module: OSFP 800G 2xDR4 (NVIDIA MMS4X00), the module in the leaf and spine switches’ cages. It carries two 400G links: one shared eight-lane DSP serves a representative photonics chip, with eight 100G transmit channels grouped on one side and eight receive channels on the other. Four channels in each direction feed each optical port. The internal placement and separate analog chips are representative, not a documented teardown. The compute trays’ own NIC ports take a different module, a single-port OSFP 400G DR4; the Switch side · NIC side toggle opens the tray end of the link. Everything that turns the host’s electrical lanes into light, and back, is inside. The other toggle also shows a half-retimed (LRO) version, with the DSP on transmit only, and the LPO version, with no DSP.
reason: Recertified 10/08/2026: supported with a disclosed assumption or limit. Footprint at published OSFP size and the module identity are sourced; the single shared eight-lane DSP and the internal partition are stated as representative, not a teardown.

label: Inside the NIC module
value: A 400G single-port optical module, opened up: its footprint drawn to its published size, its layers pulled apart vertically, its parts representative. This tray’s module: OSFP 400G DR4 (NVIDIA MMS4X00-NS400), the module in the compute tray’s NIC cages. It carries one 400G link: one DSP serves a representative photonics chip, with four 100G transmit channels grouped on one side and four receive channels on the other, all feeding one optical port. It is one DR4 engine of the twin-port module at the switch end: the same board, shell and parts, with the second engine’s lanes left out. The internal placement and separate analog chips are representative, not a documented teardown. The switch end of the link takes OSFP 800G 2xDR4 (NVIDIA MMS4X00), a twin-port; the Switch side · NIC side toggle flips between the two. label: dsp
value: In the design drawn, one DSP handles all four transmit lanes and all four receive lanes, at 100G per lane: 400G each way, to the module’s one 400G port at the fibers. On transmit, host traces enter the DSP, then line-side traces fan out to the eight-channel driver and transmit bank. On receive, the eight-channel TIA feeds this same DSP, which recovers the signals and sends the data to the host. label: mzm
value: Four Mach-Zehnder modulators, one per lane. Each splits the lasers’ light into two arms, shifts one arm with the lane’s signal and recombines them, so the light brightens and dims with the data. Waveguides carry it to the fiber edge. This is one common design: many DR4 modules use EMLs instead, a laser and modulator on one chip per lane with no shared laser, and NVIDIA’s 800G twin-port datasheet names an EML.

value: About 179k strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. label: optics
value: Every link is lit at both ends by a pluggable module, from merchant suppliers such as InnoLight and Coherent as well as NVIDIA’s own LinkX line. label: interhall
value: About 171k strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: ductbank
value: Between buildings, fiber runs in 4-inch conduits cast in concrete, one high-count ribbon cable per conduit, with a spare row. In this layout half the spine-to-core links cross between halls: about 171k strands, or roughly 25 cables of 6,912 fibers each.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: optics
value: Every link is lit at both ends by a pluggable module, from merchant suppliers such as InnoLight and Coherent as well as NVIDIA’s own LinkX line. Here they fill the faces of the leaf switches at the row ends and of the spine switches, with a link light on each and fiber rising to the runway. 1 physical scale-out link leaves the rack per GPU, and every tier above adds more modules: about 3.5 per GPU, 2.2 MW for this campus. Runs this short can also be multimode: short-reach optics on aqua fiber, rated to 50 m on OM4. A splitter (breakout) cable can also share one switch port between two adapters, each at half rate. One leaf switch here shows both: a tan-tabbed module sends two straight aqua cables to two racks, and the module beside it sends two 1:2 splitter cables to four. They are representative examples, not counted in the totals. Go inside to open this scenario’s switch module: OSFP 800G 2xDR4 (NVIDIA MMS4X00).
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: interhall
value: About 1.7 million strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: ductbank
value: Between buildings, fiber runs in 4-inch conduits cast in concrete, one high-count ribbon cable per conduit, with a spare row. In this layout half the spine-to-core links cross between halls: about 1.7 million strands, or roughly 248 cables of 6,912 fibers each.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: optics
value: Every link is lit at both ends by a pluggable module, from merchant suppliers such as InnoLight and Coherent as well as NVIDIA’s own LinkX line. Here they fill the faces of the leaf switches at the row ends and of the spine switches, with a link light on each and fiber rising to the runway. 1 physical scale-out link leaves the rack per GPU, and every tier above adds more modules: about 3.5 per GPU, 22.0 MW for this campus. Runs this short can also be multimode: short-reach optics on aqua fiber, rated to 50 m on OM4. A splitter (breakout) cable can also share one switch port between two adapters, each at half rate. One leaf switch here shows both: a tan-tabbed module sends two straight aqua cables to two racks, and the module beside it sends two 1:2 splitter cables to four. They are representative examples, not counted in the totals. Go inside to open this scenario’s switch module: OSFP 800G 2xDR4 (NVIDIA MMS4X00).
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: All of it comes back out
value: Every one of those 1 GW leaves again as heat. Chillers and cooling towers carry it away; cooling alone takes 108 MW. With the conversion losses, this design runs at PUE 1.21 and uses about 9,926 m³ of water a day (WUE is measured per kWh of IT energy, not meter energy).
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: Clean power, at a price
value: UPS modules turn AC into DC and back again so the racks never see a flicker. That double conversion costs 30 MW, more than any other power-conversion step before the rack.

label: interhall
value: About 185k strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other.

label: ductbank
value: Between buildings, fiber runs in 4-inch conduits cast in concrete, one high-count ribbon cable per conduit, with a spare row. In this layout half the spine-to-core links cross between halls: about 185k strands, or roughly 27 cables of 6,912 fibers each.

label: optics
value: Every link is lit at both ends by a pluggable module, from merchant suppliers such as InnoLight and Coherent as well as NVIDIA’s own LinkX line. Here they fill the faces of the leaf switches at the row ends and of the spine switches, with a link light on each and fiber rising to the runway. 1 physical scale-out link leaves the rack per GPU, and every tier above adds more modules: about 3.5 per GPU, 2.4 MW for this campus. Runs this short can also be multimode: short-reach optics on aqua fiber, rated to 50 m on OM4. A splitter (breakout) cable can also share one switch port between two adapters, each at half rate. One leaf switch here shows both: a tan-tabbed module sends two straight aqua cables to two racks, and the module beside it sends two 1:2 splitter cables to four. They are representative examples, not counted in the totals. Go inside to open this scenario’s switch module: OSFP 800G 2xDR4 (NVIDIA MMS4X00).

label: ductbank
value: Between buildings, fiber runs in 4-inch conduits cast in concrete, one high-count ribbon cable per conduit, with a spare row. In this layout half the spine-to-core links cross between halls: about 1.8 million strands, or roughly 268 cables of 6,912 fibers each.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: optics
value: Every link is lit at both ends by a pluggable module, from merchant suppliers such as InnoLight and Coherent as well as NVIDIA’s own LinkX line. Here they fill the faces of the leaf switches at the row ends and of the spine switches, with a link light on each and fiber rising to the runway. 1 physical scale-out link leaves the rack per GPU, and every tier above adds more modules: about 3.5 per GPU, 23.8 MW for this campus. Runs this short can also be multimode: short-reach optics on aqua fiber, rated to 50 m on OM4. A splitter (breakout) cable can also share one switch port between two adapters, each at half rate. One leaf switch here shows both: a tan-tabbed module sends two straight aqua cables to two racks, and the module beside it sends two 1:2 splitter cables to four. They are representative examples, not counted in the totals. Go inside to open this scenario’s switch module: OSFP 800G 2xDR4 (NVIDIA MMS4X00).
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: 345,000 volts

label: interhall
value: About 9.2 million strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: optics

value: Every link is lit at both ends by a pluggable module, from merchant suppliers such as InnoLight and Coherent as well as NVIDIA’s own LinkX line. Runs this short can also be multimode: short-reach optics on aqua fiber, rated to 50 m on OM4. A splitter (breakout) cable can also share one switch port between two adapters, each at half rate. One leaf switch here shows both: a tan-tabbed module sends two straight aqua cables to two racks, and the module beside it sends two 1:2 splitter cables to four. value: A 1.6T twin-port optical module, opened up: its footprint drawn to its published size, its layers pulled apart vertically, its parts representative. This scenario’s switch module: OSFP 1.6T 2xDR4 (NVIDIA MMS4A00), the module in the leaf and spine switches’ cages. It carries two 800G links: one shared eight-lane DSP serves a representative photonics chip, with eight 200G transmit channels grouped on one side and eight receive channels on the other. Four channels in each direction feed each optical port. The internal placement and separate analog chips are representative, not a documented teardown. The compute trays’ own NIC ports take a different module, a single-port OSFP 800G DR4; the Switch side · NIC side toggle opens the tray end of the link. Everything that turns the host’s electrical lanes into light, and back, is inside. The other toggle also shows a half-retimed (LRO) version, with the DSP on transmit only, and the LPO version, with no DSP.

This tray’s module: OSFP 800G DR4 (NVIDIA single-port 800G OSFP DR4), the module in the compute tray’s NIC cages. It carries one 800G link: one DSP serves a representative photonics chip, with four 200G transmit channels grouped on one side and four receive channels on the other, all feeding one optical port. label: interhall
value: About 1.6 million strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: interhall
value: About 11.4 million strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: ductbank

reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: interhall
value: About 11.0 million strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: interhall
value: About 856k strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: optics

label: interhall
value: About 611k strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: Standing by

label: All of it comes back out

label: home
value: SpaceXAI (formerly xAI). This page rebuilds the campus from the closest scenario it can: GPU counts come from Elon Musk’s post (09/25/2026). The halls, CDUs, cables, token rates and the whole layout are this model’s, sized from those counts, not SpaceXAI’s. Meter power is this model’s estimate from those counts: each accelerator’s own bottom-up rack power, plus its network, at this design’s PUE. It lands above Epoch AI’s ≈946 MW satellite estimate of IT power from a day earlier, which counted 440,000 chips. The 3D rack, tray and package show a GB300 NVL72, the chip in four of five GPUs. The 110,000 GB200s are counted in every total at their own rack power, memory and transistor count, not as GB300s. Each accelerator runs its own scale-out fabric at its own NIC speed (GB200 at 400G, GB300 at 800G). How SpaceXAI actually connects them is not public; Elon Musk ties the 110k figure to what one central switch can take. Stages after Now are what Elon Musk said is coming, not installed hardware; the last is contingent (“if we get lucky”). Backup is modeled as batteries only, since SpaceXAI lists a battery pack and mentions no diesel. The 3.3 GWh pack is planned and its power rating is not published, so the model assumes it can carry the whole campus; its hours at full load shrink as the fleet grows. Cooling is modeled as air-cooled chillers (as SemiAnalysis counted in 08/2025) on a closed loop, as SpaceXAI describes Colossus II, so the model counts no cooling water; SpaceXAI says the site takes only domestic water. Liquid-cooled racks on that plant are inferred from the GB200 and GB300 designs, not confirmed. Elon Musk’s 550,000 (110k GB200 + 440k GB300) and Epoch’s satellite count a day earlier (110k GB200 + 330k GB300 = 440,000) disagree on the GB300 share; this page shows both and is sized from Elon Musk’s count. xAI became SpaceXAI in July 2026 (see Colossus 1’s unknowns); most sources cited here still say “xAI”. An earlier pass of this page stated the site’s “first plan” was “≈1 GW, ≈350,000 GPUs”; the ≈350,000-GPU figure could not be traced to any source and was dropped rather than kept as an unsupported number. Go in to follow the power down.

label: home
value: Microsoft. This page rebuilds the campus from the closest scenario it can: Meter power is estimated from the ≈636 MW IT figure at a PUE near 1.15. The GB200/GB300 split is not disclosed; GB300 is assumed. Closed-loop liquid is modeled as warm water with dry coolers on a closed loop, as Microsoft describes it, so the model counts no cooling water and no hot-day sprays; how the plant rides out the hottest afternoons is not stated in the sources here. Microsoft says the design forgoes on-site generation, UPS systems and dual-corded distribution for the GPU fleet. This preset still runs the model’s generic power chain, with its UPS losses, generators and batteries, so those figures are the generic model’s, not Microsoft’s. Go in to follow the power down.

label: interhall
value: About 1.1 million strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: interhall
value: About 804k strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: optics
value: Every link is lit at both ends by a pluggable module, from merchant suppliers such as InnoLight and Coherent as well as NVIDIA’s own LinkX line. Here they fill the faces of the leaf switches at the row ends and of the spine switches, with a link light on each and fiber rising to the runway. 1 physical scale-out link leaves the rack per GPU, and every tier above adds more modules: about 3.5 per GPU, 10.4 MW for this campus. Runs this short can also be multimode: short-reach optics on aqua fiber, rated to 50 m on OM4. A splitter (breakout) cable can also share one switch port between two adapters, each at half rate. One leaf switch here shows both: a tan-tabbed module sends two straight aqua cables to two racks, and the module beside it sends two 1:2 splitter cables to four. They are representative examples, not counted in the totals. Go inside to open this scenario’s switch module: OSFP 800G 2xDR4 (NVIDIA MMS4X00).

label: optics
value: Every link is lit at both ends by a pluggable module, from merchant suppliers such as InnoLight and Coherent as well as NVIDIA’s own LinkX line. Here they fill the faces of the leaf switches at the row ends and of the spine switches, with a link light on each and fiber rising to the runway. 1 physical scale-out link leaves the rack per GPU, and every tier above adds more modules: about 3.5 per GPU, 34.5 MW for this campus. label: home
value: Amazon Web Services (built for Anthropic). This page rebuilds the campus from the closest scenario it can: This site's engine models NVIDIA accelerators only; Project Rainier runs AWS's own Trainium2 chips (UltraServers of 64 chips each), which it cannot model, so the closest preset by rack power and cooling is used instead — H100-class, air-cooled, 415 V AC — and its watts-per-chip and per-rack figures are NVIDIA's, not Amazon's real silicon. Meter power is estimated from the ≈910 MW IT figure at a PUE near 1.15, the value reported for this chiller-free, air-cooled design. The Trainium2-to-Trainium3 mix as later buildings come online is not modeled; all live capacity is treated as one class. Building counts vary by source (30 per company figures, up to 32 in Epoch's imagery-based count, ≈18 per Compute Atlas); this page follows Epoch's 16-of-32-live split. Go in to follow the power down.

label: interhall
value: About 2.1 million strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: ductbank
value: Between buildings, fiber runs in 4-inch conduits cast in concrete, one high-count ribbon cable per conduit, with a spare row. In this layout half the spine-to-core links cross between halls: about 2.1 million strands, or roughly 310 cables of 6,912 fibers each.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: spine
value: The spine connects every leaf to every other. Two tiers of 64-port switches reach about 2,048 GPUs; this campus uses 3, in 9 parallel planes.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: optics
value: Every link is lit at both ends by a pluggable module, from merchant suppliers such as InnoLight and Coherent as well as NVIDIA’s own LinkX line. Here they fill the faces of the leaf switches at the row ends and of the spine switches, with a link light on each and fiber rising to the runway. 1 physical scale-out link leaves the rack per GPU, and every tier above adds more modules: about 3.0 per GPU, 27.5 MW for this campus. Runs this short can also be multimode: short-reach optics on aqua fiber, rated to 50 m on OM4. A splitter (breakout) cable can also share one switch port between two adapters, each at half rate. Go inside to open this scenario’s switch module: OSFP 800G 2xDR4 (NVIDIA MMS4X00).

label: Standing by

label: interhall
value: About 1.0 million strands in the duct banks join the spines of every hall, so a single training job can span every GPU on the campus. Each link needs optics rated for its length. The two halls drawn here sit about 140 m apart at their spine ends, inside the 500 m of the same parallel-fiber DR optics used within a hall. Longer runs between buildings step up to FR4 (2 km) or LR4 (10 km), which put four wavelengths on one fiber pair, each carrying four-level PAM4 signals rather than the coherent ones used between campuses; DR and FR4 modules cannot be linked to each other. The plain hall blocks farther out are not routed here, so their link lengths are not modeled.

label: optics

label: How much heat each part is drawn with
value: log scale: each 10× in power is 5× the motion; nothing under 0.5 W: Parts in one view span about a watt to about a kilowatt, so heat motion (how many pulses, how big, how bright) is drawn on a log scale: each part’s motion is its watts divided by the largest source’s in the same view, raised to the power log10(5) ≈ 0.7, so every 10× in power is the same step, 5× the motion. A 1 kW chip and a 10 W chip in one view differ about 25×; rank order always holds, and a part drawing more power never shows less heat than one drawing less. Parts under half a watt (photodiodes, modulator bias, a passive copper cable’s ID memory, fibers and connectors) draw no heat at all. Coolant and air loops are compared with each other, by the heat they carry, and each view keeps its total motion within a fixed budget, so a busy view is scaled down as a whole, its ratios kept. label: How much each part glows in the Power layer
value: log scale, per view: each 10× in power is 5× the glow; nothing under 0.5 W: In the Power layer every part that draws electrical power wears a soft halo around its footprint, on the same log rule as the heat drawing (heat-visual-scale): a part’s glow is its watts divided by the largest draw in the same view, raised to the power log10(5) ≈ 0.7, and the halo’s brightness and reach each take the square root of that, so every 10× in power is the same step and a part drawing more never glows less than one drawing less. Parts under half a watt (a passive copper cable end, photodiode and modulator bias) do not glow, and passive parts never do: fibers, MPO and cable assemblies as such, passive optics, heat sinks, cold plates, connectors, busbars, busways and stored-energy batteries. Equipment that passes power on glows by what it loses doing so: voltage regulators, bus converters, power shelves and supplies, UPS modules, transformers and switchgear. Where a level compares variants (the module’s full DSP, LRO and LPO, the CPO level’s two packages), the reference stays the full design, so a variant that draws less glows less. Watts are the heat drawing’s, the model’s power ledger for transformer, UPS and solid-state transformer losses, the fabric table for modules and switches, and these further order-of-magnitude allocations, used only for the glow: a module’s or 800ZR’s converters ≈2 W, an external laser module ≈5 W, a soldered LPDDR5X package ≈2 W, a PCIe switch ≈25 W, a CDU’s pumps about 1% of the heat it moves, fans about 3% of the heat their air carries, low-voltage switchgear about 0.1% of what passes through it; a tray’s NIC and DPU power, and its drive, fan and management power, are split evenly over the parts that draw them. Only ratios within a view matter. The halo’s slow breathing is decoration and stops with reduced motion; views without bloom draw it a little brighter, and Battery saver leaves out the faintest halos.

label: 1. What the model is, and what it is not
value:
This page carries one scenario model of one campus. Its hardware follows from four choices: campus size at the meter, accelerator generation, power design to the rack, and cooling design. For a generic campus, hardware counts and power are derived from those four choices by compute(scenario) in src/model/engine.ts. Change a choice and that whole model recomputes; reported site fleets and plant overrides provide additional inputs for named campuses.

Tokens and energy per token (Section 8) sit on top of that hardware model rather than following from it alone: they add their own workload and environment inputs, tokens per GPU per second, utilization, a grid-carbon figure, and a training-energy assumption, set in src/model/tokens.js. The Evidence page shows one fixed reference scenario for its claims and sources; it does not follow whatever campus you have set here.

This page is not a bill of materials for a real, named building. No vendor has published a construction drawing for any campus on this page, and this model does not claim to reproduce one. Where a real campus is picked as a preset (Section 9), the model rebuilds the closest scenario it can from disclosed facts, and says plainly which of the four choices had to be assumed rather than confirmed.

The model conserves energy by construction: every megawatt drawn at the meter is accounted for in the ledger (Section 3) plus what reaches the GPU silicon, down to floating-point rounding. src/model/engine.test.ts checks this for every accelerator, power design and cooling choice at once.
reason: Corrected stale description against implementation; remaining source-backed sentences are not fully recertified.

label: 3. Power: how rack power and PUE come out of the meter
value:
Rack power is built bottom-up, one rack at a time, in kilowatts. Package power comes first: pkgKW = accel.gpuW * accel.gpusPerRack / 1000, split into an HBM share (accel.hbmShare) and GPU silicon. Voltage regulation loss follows from the regulator's own efficiency: vrmLossKW = pkgKW / accel.vrmEff - pkgKW. GPU package power, its VRM loss, CPU power, NVLink switching (scaleupKW), NICs (nicKW) and the rest (otherKW) sum into a 12 V board load (load12), which the bus converter's efficiency (accel.ibcEff) turns into a small further loss, then a busbar loss (busbarKW), then a final rack-level conversion (accel.psuEff on AC, or EFF.rackDcDc on 800 V DC) to reach the full rack draw, rack.kw.

At the facility level the engine solves for IT power rather than assuming a PUE. It writes one equation, meter times the upstream efficiency equals IT power divided by the IT conversion path, plus cooling and building loads divided by the cooling/building path, and solves it for IT_MW. PUE, meterMW / IT_MW, falls out of that solve; it is never set directly. What is set directly is each conversion step's efficiency and each cooling design's coolFrac, chosen so the whole chain lands the design in its published PUE band (air near 1.5, chilled liquid 1.10 to 1.20, warm water 1.05 to 1.15).

The ledger the page shows (compute().ledger) turns each of these losses into a megawatt figure at campus scale, with gpuSiliconMW calculated from the installed GPU packages minus their assumed HBM share. A generic campus's unused power budget is recorded separately as unallocated capacity, not GPU silicon. engine.test.ts checks that the ledger's rows plus GPU silicon always sum back to the meter, to nine decimal places, for every accelerator, power and cooling combination.

label: 4. Racks, GPUs and halls
value:
Rack and GPU counts follow from IT power, not the other way around. A fabric tier's cost per GPU (tierConfig(tiers).kwPerGpu) depends only on the tier count, not on how many GPUs the campus ends up with, so the engine solves for racks directly instead of guessing and re-checking: racks = Math.floor(IT_MW * 1000 / (rackKW + accel.gpusPerRack * fab.kwPerGpu)) with a two-tier fabric's cost first. If the GPU count that buys actually fits a two-tier fabric's own non-blocking port budget, that is the final rack count; if the site's power would buy more GPUs than two tiers can carry, the same formula is solved again with a three-tier fabric's higher (so always more conservative) per-GPU cost, and that is final. GPU count is simply racks * accel.gpusPerRack.

Data halls are sized at roughly 45 MW of IT load each: halls = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(IT_MW / 45)). This is the model's own working assumption, not a vendor figure, and it is the number the campus scene uses to decide how many hall blocks to draw. Everything downstream in the layout, transformer counts, generator counts, chiller or dry-cooler counts, cooling distribution units, is sized the same way: from a power figure (meter, IT, or cooling power) divided by a typical catalog unit size, then rounded up, in layout at the end of compute().
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: 5. The network: fat-tree sizing
value:
Fabric sizing keys off NIC speed. FABRICS in engine.ts holds three speed classes, 400G, 800G and 1600G, each with a switch radix, a switch power draw, and per-port and per-GPU optics power. GB200 defaults to the 400G class, NVIDIA's own reference design of one 400G ConnectX-7 port per GPU: a 64-port switch (radix: 64, NVIDIA's Quantum-2 QM9700) drawing 0.75 kW. GB300's documented ConnectX-8 upgrade uses the 800G class instead, a 144-port switch (radix: 144) drawing 2.9 kW, with a 17 W GPU-side module and a 13.5 W port-side module, two ports per module, 8 fibers per link.

tierConfig(tiers) gives each tier count's per-GPU port, link and switch-power cost from that radix; a two-tier, non-blocking fat tree fits up to radix² / 2 GPUs. The engine tries two tiers first, and only falls back to three (up to radix³ / 4 GPUs, and beyond that parallel fabric planes, planes = Math.ceil(G / threeTierMax)) when the GPU count a two-tier fabric would actually buy exceeds its own port budget — which a three-tier fabric's costlier, more conservative per-GPU price can never do in turn, so the choice needs no further checking once made. Two tiers cost each GPU 3 ports and 2 links; three tiers cost 5 ports and 3 links, because traffic now crosses leaf, spine and core.

Switch counts follow directly: leaf = Math.ceil(gpus / (radix / 2)), spine and core by the same division at each tier, and switches = leaf + spine + core. Links are gpus * fab.linksPerGpu, and fibers are links * fibersPerLink. Modules per GPU work out to 1 at the GPU-side NIC plus, in a two-tier build, 3 switch ports carried on twin-port modules, for 1 + 3/2 = 2.5; a three-tier build with 5 ports per GPU comes to 3.5 — the figure engine.test.ts checks directly for the 100 MW reference scenario, which at GB200's 400G fabric is itself a three-tier build. Scale-across fiber (the DCI block) is sized separately at roughly 10 Gb/s per GPU to other sites, converted into a number of lit wavelength pairs at 32 lambdas of 800 Gb/s each.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: 6. Heat and water
value:
Cooling power and water use are both set by the cooling choice, not computed from first principles. Each entry in COOLING carries a coolFrac, cooling power as a fraction of IT load, and a wue, liters of water per kilowatt-hour of energy delivered.

CoolingcoolFracwue (L/kWh)Design PUE band it targets
Air-cooled halls with chillers0.421.0≈1.5
Liquid to the chip, chilled water0.130.51.10–1.20
Warm-water liquid, dry coolers0.080.161.05–1.15

Both columns are the model's own calibration, chosen so that once the power chain's own losses (Section 3) are added on top, each design lands in its published PUE band; the code comment above COOLING says so directly. Water use then follows arithmetically, but against IT power rather than meter power: waterM3h = IT_MW * wue (engine.ts's waterM3h helper), because The Green Grid defines WUE as liters per kilowatt-hour of IT equipment energy, not facility energy — the two differ by a factor of PUE, so using meter power here would overstate water use by however much the design's PUE exceeds 1. On a hot day (clock.ts) it rises further once outdoor air reaches a shared adiabatic-assist threshold, 35°C, for warm-water designs, or as chiller efficiency falls roughly 2.5% per degree above 25°C for chilled designs; that threshold and the design's chilled-water and warm-water supply temperatures live in one place, engine.ts's WATER constant, so the cards and the clock never disagree on what the design assumes.

Every other temperature the page names, from the die to the outside air, comes from one operating point per cooling design built on those constants, loopTemps() in engine.ts (the assumption "One operating point for the cooling loops"). A liquid design has two loops that meet at the CDU: the rack loop warms about 10 °C across a rack, facility water runs about 3 °C below it on each side, and a die sits about 20 °C above the coolant leaving its cold plate. An air design has one chilled-water loop between the in-row coils and the chillers, with 22 °C supply air and an 18 °C rise through the servers. The heat tour, the cards and the Hot to cold chart all read this one set, and each figure says which loop it is on and whether it is the supply or the return. Only NVIDIA's 45 °C warm-water inlet and ≈55 °C outlet, and ASHRAE's 18–27 °C supply-air band, are published; the rest is illustrative.

label: 7. Time: the four clocks
value:
src/model/clock.ts samples the same static model over time along four independent clocks, each a pure function of (model, time):

ClockTimescaleWhat it assumes
Training stepseconds (a 60 s window)GPU load swings in a 2-second step with a 0.35 low point and a checkpoint pause at 38–44 s; rests on the 0.2–3 Hz swing band a joint Microsoft/OpenAI/NVIDIA measurement paper found in production clusters (spec). For GB300 and Vera Rubin, a rack-level capacitor buffer (trainingStorage) aims for a low-pass target (τ ≈ 0.6 s, an estimate) but is held to NVIDIA's stated 65 J/GPU capacity and an estimated charge/discharge rate: past that limit it stops tracking the target and the raw swing shows through, exactly what the tiny real capacity does across a multi-second checkpoint. A second buffer, the site batteries, does the same against their own rating (layout.bessMW) and a far larger capacity, so what the grid actually sees can still show part of a swing neither buffer could absorb.
Grid outageseconds, then minutesGrid fails at t=5 s; generators ramp up to carry the full load by t=15 s, matching NFPA 110's Type 10 timing class (Level 1 is a separate classification, for loads whose loss could cost lives — data-center IT is not itself one, but many mission-critical campuses design to Type 10 timing anyway); batteries bridge the gap until then, including the last couple of seconds of the generators' own ramp; chillers (non-warm designs) take about 2 minutes to restart; the grid returns 15 minutes in and the site waits 5 more minutes of stability before transferring back. Sample.meterMW is the utility import alone (zero while islanded); Sample.siteMW is what the site actually draws from every source, the figure the live counters integrate for site-wide energy. The chiller restart time, the outage length and the stability window are this page's own illustrative choices.
Hot day24 hoursOutdoor temperature follows a cosine curve, coolest near 3 a.m., hottest at 3 p.m., with a 16°C swing by default; warm-water designs hold steady until air crosses 35°C, then adiabatic sprays add water; chilled designs lose roughly 2.5% cooling efficiency per degree above 25°C. No sourced dry-cooler derating curve was found, so these slopes are estimates.
Inference day24 hoursDemand follows a qualitative shape drawn from measurement studies of real LLM services, overnight trough, morning rise, midday dip, afternoon peak, evening decline, with a default 2.5× peak-to-trough ratio and GPUs idling at 30% of full power. No hyperscaler has published a peak-to-trough ratio, so that number is explicitly illustrative in the code and on the page.

label: 8. Tokens and energy per token
value:
src/model/tokens.js holds the reader's own settings in one object, calc: tokens per GPU per second (defaulting to an accelerator-specific reference, see below), utilization (0.6 default), a grid carbon figure (370 g CO₂/kWh, close to the US average of 373), a training energy allowance (50 GWh) amortized over a model's lifetime output (10¹⁵ tokens by default), and whether training's share is included at all.

tokenFigures(M, c) computes a serving rate, M.gpus * tps * c.util, then joules per token from two sources: jOps = meterMW * 1e6 / rate, the campus's whole draw divided by tokens served, and jTrain = c.trainGWh * 3.6e12 / c.lifeTokens, training energy spread across a model's lifetime tokens. The two sum to total joules per token; a 500-token reply's watt-hours, carbon and water then follow by simple unit conversion. The watt-hours are meter energy, cooling included; the water figure divides them by PUE first, because the wue that governs the cooling chart is defined on IT energy.

The request tour adds its own timeline on top: 25 ms across the internet each way, 50 ms in a queue, 200 ms of prefill and 60 tokens a second for one user's stream. Those are a separate illustrative assumption ("An illustrative request timeline"), the same for every accelerator, not a benchmark of the hardware selected; only the energy and water per reply come from the scenario.

The reference tokens-per-GPU figure, tokPerGpuRef in engine.ts, is Math.round(2000 * accel.hbm.tbs / 8 / 50) * 50: it scales with HBM bandwidth on the reasoning that decode, generating one token at a time, is memory-bound rather than compute-bound, so a GPU with twice the memory bandwidth of another can plausibly serve roughly twice the tokens per second. This is the model's own derived estimate, not a benchmark result for any specific accelerator.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: 10. The basis labels, and how a figure earns each
value:
Every figure the page shows beside a basis chip carries one of five labels, defined in src/evidence.js's BASIS object: spec, the maker or a standards body states this exact figure for the named product or standard, backed by at least one primary source; vendor, a vendor's own comparison or performance claim, attributed to it and stating what it's measured against, not checked independently here; reported, a named third party — a government agency, a researcher, an analyst, or the trade press — states it; derived, this page's model calculates it from the scenario and its cited inputs; and assumed, the model chose a value where no single published figure applies. Two earlier labels, "Typical" and "Est.", are on the way out: they mark a figure not yet traced to one of the five, and tools/claims.mjs's strict pass fails on any that remain within the prefixes it's told to check.

Evidence rides with the claim, not just the label. A spec, vendor or reported figure carries a refs list of [sourceId, where] pairs, pointing at a section, table, page or figure in a source listed in src/sources.js — a spec needs at least one of those sources marked primary. A derived figure names a calc id; its formula is written out once in CALCS, in src/evidence.js, and repeated nowhere else. An assumed figure names an assume id; its reasoning lives the same way in ASSUMPTIONS. Both registries are reproduced in full below (Sections 13 and 14), so a reader never has to open the source to see why a number is what it is. Clicking any basis chip on the page opens that one claim's own popover; the Evidence page lists every claim for one reference scenario, and tools/claims.mjs runs the same strict checks on every claim across all 104 scenarios.
reason: Not individually recertified in the blocked audit. Source retrieval and metadata validity alone do not establish this claim; independent calculation coverage is not yet exhaustive.

label: 11. Known gaps and estimates the site carries
value:
The research files in research/ name these gaps directly, and the model's numbers reflect them rather than papering over them:

  • No sourced peak-to-trough ratio exists for inference traffic; the model's 2.5× default is stated as illustrative in both the code comment and the page's own notes.
  • No named vendor dry-cooler derating curve was found; the hot-day clock's cooling-power slopes are estimates, flagged as such in clock.ts's own notes.
  • Bus-converter and voltage-regulator efficiency at the board level (the 50 V/54 V to 12 V step, and 12 V to the GPU core) have no published vendor figure for any of these accelerators; every number in that part of the ledger is labeled Assumed, with its reasoning in Section 14.
  • HBM's share of total GPU power (10–16% across generations, applied per accelerator as hbmShare) is this model's own assumption. No vendor publishes it, and the paper once cited for it measures only relative power and gives no such share.
  • NVIDIA's own claim for 800 V DC is "up to 5% end-to-end efficiency gain"; a separately circulated "83% to 92%" framing is a different, unconfirmed construction and this model uses only NVIDIA's own figure, which engine.test.ts checks the DC-800 scenario against directly.
  • GB200's per-GPU NVLink figure has a direct-fetch anomaly in NVIDIA's own material (1.8 TB/s versus a 3.6 TB/s figure on the same page); the model uses 1.8 TB/s, the figure corroborated everywhere else.
  • No single sourced ratio exists for gensets or unit substations per 100 MW; the counts in layout (for example gensets = Math.ceil(meterMW / 3 * 1.2), a 3 MW class unit at N+20%) are this model's own sizing, not an industry-standard ratio.
  • Microsoft's own post says Fairwater Atlanta forgoes on-site generation, UPS systems and dual-corded distribution for its GPU fleet. The preset still runs the model's generic power chain, UPS and generators included, and says so in its unknowns.
reason: Corrected stale description against implementation; remaining source-backed sentences are not fully recertified.

label: 12. How the site is tested
value:
The Vitest suite gates model correctness. Four of its core files are described here. engine.test.ts checks energy conservation (ledger plus GPU silicon equals the meter, to nine decimal places, for every accelerator, power and cooling combination), that bottom-up rack power lands within the published range for each accelerator, that cooling choices land in and stay ordered within their published PUE bands, that 800 V DC's IT-power gain over AC stays inside NVIDIA's own "up to 5%" claim, and that the fabric never falls short of the ports it needs. clock.test.ts samples all four clocks across every scenario at 300 points each and checks every value is finite, non-negative and inside a sane range. data.test.ts generates the page's full text content for every scenario, every real-campus preset, and a spread of campus sizes, and checks no string is empty, undefined or NaN, and every number on the page carries a valid basis. journeys.test.ts checks every beat of every guided tour, across the same scenario spread, is complete and lands on a real part in the 3D scene, and that no tour skips a level or returns to one it has left.

The tools/ scripts test the rendered page itself, on the real GPU, rather than the model's arithmetic: cycle.mjs, views.mjs and links.mjs walk every scenario, scene and tour stop and check nothing errors, every view is unobstructed, and every link lands where it claims to; perf.mjs measures frame cost, draw calls and triangle counts; ui.mjs checks on-screen controls never overlap at desktop or phone size; coplanar.mjs and flicker.mjs catch z-fighting; gpushot.mjs, hero.mjs, look.mjs and shot.mjs capture screenshots for review. npm test runs the Vitest suite; the tools run by hand against a live dev server.
reason: Corrected stale description against implementation; remaining source-backed sentences are not fully recertified.

value: An 800G optical module is a small assembly line: a connector, a chip that cleans up the signal, a laser that turns it into light, and a receiver that turns light back into a signal. LPO saves power by removing that signal-processing chip outright, so the host's own SerDes drives and reads the line directly. CPO saves power a different way, by shortening the electrical run between the switch chip and the optics and cutting out the pluggable module and its connector — not necessarily by deleting the signal-processing chip too. See the pluggable module and co-packaged optics in 3D.
